prompt: A global ticketing platform needs a database for inventory and transactions. Requirements: strong external consistency, horizontal scalability across regions, SQL support, and 99.999% availability for a multi-region deployment. Which managed service best fits?

choices.text: Cloud Bigtable with replicated clusters in several regions
choices.rationale: Bigtable is a wide-column NoSQL store. Multi-cluster instances are eventually consistent by default, and although GoogleSQL queries are available, the data model is not the relational, strongly consistent transactional one an inventory ledger needs.

choices.text: Cloud Spanner using a multi-region instance configuration
choices.rationale: Spanner is relational with SQL, scales horizontally, provides external consistency (stronger than plain strong consistency), and multi-region configurations carry a 99.999% availability target. It is the only option that meets all four requirements.

choices.text: Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL with a cross-region read replica
choices.rationale: Read replicas replicate asynchronously and are read-only, so reads from the remote replica are eventually consistent, writes still funnel through one primary, and replicas provide no failover. It cannot deliver strong consistency across regions at five-nines.

choices.text: Firestore in Datastore mode with a multi-region location
choices.rationale: Datastore mode is a NoSQL entity store, not a relational SQL database. It can be strongly consistent, but it does not give the SQL relational model the platform requires.

prompt: Altostrat Media's GKE content platform serves the media library from Cloud Storage and relies on catalog and entitlements data. After a regional outage, leadership mandates an RTO of minutes and an RPO near zero for the catalog and entitlements data. Cost control is a top priority, and the budget cannot justify running full-capacity compute in two regions at all times. Which disaster-recovery pattern matches these constraints most cost-effectively?

choices.text: Scheduled backups to Cloud Storage, restored into a rebuilt environment after the outage
choices.rationale: The RPO is bounded by the backup interval and the RTO includes rebuilding and restoring, which typically takes hours. This is the cheapest pattern but misses both targets.

choices.text: Cold standby in a second region, with infrastructure provisioned only after disaster declaration
choices.rationale: A cold pattern has the longest recovery time and no continuous replication, so provisioning after declaration cannot achieve an RTO of minutes or a near-zero RPO.

choices.text: Warm standby in a second region: a scaled-down replica fed by continuous replication, scaled up on failover
choices.rationale: Continuous replication keeps the RPO near zero, and a scaled-down footprint that scales up on failover reaches an RTO of minutes without paying for a full duplicate fleet at all times. It sits between the cold and hot patterns on cost.

choices.text: Hot active-active across two regions, with full-capacity compute serving production traffic in each region
choices.rationale: A hot pattern meets both targets because both environments serve production traffic, but it runs full capacity in two regions at all times. It is the most expensive pattern, which the stated budget rules out.

explanation: Match the pattern to the RTO/RPO targets: smaller objectives cost more, so pay for only as much standby capacity as the targets require.

prompt: You are designing private connectivity between an on-premises data center and Google Cloud for a workload that must reach Google APIs (Cloud Storage, BigQuery) without traversing the public internet, with predictable bandwidth and a high SLA. Which two choices belong in this design? Choose two.

choices.text: Dedicated or Partner Interconnect for the private link between the data center and Google
choices.rationale: Interconnect provides a private connection that bypasses the public internet, with dedicated or provisioned capacity and an end-to-end SLA, which meets the predictable-bandwidth requirement.

choices.text: Cloud VPN tunnels over the public internet as the only connectivity path to Google Cloud
choices.rationale: Cloud VPN is encrypted but runs over the public internet and suits lower bandwidth needs. It does carry an availability SLA, so the real gap is that it contradicts the no-public-internet, predictable-bandwidth requirement.

choices.text: Private Google Access for on-premises hosts, using the restricted or private googleapis VIPs over that link
choices.rationale: On-premises hosts resolve Google API names to the private.googleapis.com or restricted.googleapis.com VIPs and send the traffic over the VPN or Interconnect link, so API calls stay on private addressing and Google's network.

choices.text: External IP addresses on every VM that calls the APIs, with default internet routes to reach them
choices.rationale: External IPs and default internet routes send the traffic out through the public internet path, the opposite of what the requirement asks for.

choices.text: Cloud NAT to give the on-premises hosts outbound internet access to reach the APIs
choices.rationale: Cloud NAT provides outbound internet access, so it adds a public-internet path rather than removing it, and it is not a mechanism for private API reachability.

prompt: A team is deploying stateless HTTP microservices and wants minimal operational overhead: scale to zero when idle, billing tied to requests, and no nodes or control plane to manage. They have no need for DaemonSets, custom schedulers or sidecar service meshes. Which compute option is the best fit?

choices.text: Compute Engine managed instance groups with autoscaling behind a load balancer
choices.rationale: MIGs give you VMs to size, patch and scale. They can only scale to zero under limited autoscaling signals and bill for VM time, not requests, so they carry the most operational overhead.

choices.text: Cloud Run services with request-based billing and a minimum of zero instances
choices.rationale: Cloud Run runs stateless containers, scales to zero by default when a revision gets no traffic, bills per request by default, and has no nodes or cluster to manage.

choices.text: GKE Standard clusters with cluster autoscaler and horizontal pod autoscaling
choices.rationale: On Standard clusters the autoscaler never automatically scales the cluster to zero nodes because system Pods need at least one node, and you still manage node pools and upgrades.

choices.text: App Engine flexible environment services using automatic scaling and Docker containers
choices.rationale: Flexible keeps a minimum of one instance running and starts instances in minutes, so you pay for idle capacity. App Engine standard can scale to zero, flexible cannot.

prompt: An enterprise is building its Google Cloud landing zone. They want centrally enforced guardrails (e.g., restrict resource locations, disable external IPs, enforce uniform bucket-level access) that apply to every current and future project, inherited automatically. Which mechanism should they use?

choices.text: IAM allow policies granted on every project through a deployment pipeline
choices.rationale: IAM answers who can do what. It does not restrict how resources are configured, so it cannot block external IPs or force locations.

choices.text: Organization Policy constraints set on the organization or a top-level folder
choices.rationale: Constraints such as gcp.resourceLocations, compute.vmExternalIpAccess and storage.uniformBucketLevelAccess are inherited by all descendants, including projects created later, which is exactly the central guardrail model.

choices.text: VPC firewall rules maintained centrally in a Shared VPC host project for all service projects
choices.rationale: Firewall rules filter network traffic. They have no effect on resource configuration such as bucket access mode or allowed locations.

choices.text: Per-project budgets with billing alerts sent to the platform team each month
choices.rationale: Budgets and alerts give cost visibility after the fact. They do not prevent a resource from being created with a disallowed configuration.

prompt: Your organization wants repeatable, version-controlled, declarative provisioning of cloud infrastructure with a managed state and the ability to preview changes before applying them, using Google's recommended IaC approach. Which option should you standardize on?

choices.text: gcloud shell scripts checked into Git and executed by a CI pipeline on each merge
choices.rationale: Scripts are imperative: there is no managed state, no reconciliation against what exists, and no plan or preview, so drift and partial failures go unnoticed.

choices.text: Terraform configurations in Git, applied through Infrastructure Manager or with remote state in Cloud Storage
choices.rationale: Terraform is declarative and version-controlled. Infrastructure Manager is Google's managed Terraform service and stores state per deployment and can preview changes before applying; a Cloud Storage backend gives self-run Terraform shared state.

choices.text: Console changes recorded in a spreadsheet and exported as screenshots for audit
choices.rationale: Console work is manual, not repeatable, and leaves no code that can be reviewed, versioned or replayed.

choices.text: Scheduled Cloud Functions calling the REST APIs imperatively to create missing resources
choices.rationale: Hand-rolled API calls reimplement what an IaC tool does, without a plan step or state tracking, and are brittle to change.

prompt: You are provisioning a Shared VPC so multiple service projects can use centrally managed subnets. Which two statements are correct about the setup? Choose two.

choices.text: The VPC network, subnets and firewall rules are owned by the host project
choices.rationale: In Shared VPC the host project owns the network resources and service projects cannot create or manage them.

choices.text: Every service project builds its own VPC and peers it with the host project network
choices.rationale: That describes VPC Network Peering, a different topology. Shared VPC is a hub-and-spoke model in which service projects do not keep their own networks.

choices.text: Service project principals get Compute Network User on the host project or on specific subnets
choices.rationale: The compute.networkUser role is what lets service project principals create resources in the shared subnets; it can be granted project-wide or per subnet.

choices.text: The host and service projects must belong to different organizations for isolation
choices.rationale: They cannot belong to different organizations, apart from a temporary exception during organization migrations.

choices.text: Firewall rules must be recreated inside each service project so that traffic can flow
choices.rationale: Firewall rules are defined once in the host project and apply to the shared network, so duplicating them in service projects is neither needed nor possible.

prompt: You must provision a fleet of identical, self-healing, autoscaling Compute Engine VMs behind a load balancer, where instances are recreated automatically if they fail health checks. Which combination should you provision?

choices.text: Individually created VMs configured with startup scripts and registered behind the load balancer
choices.rationale: Standalone VMs have no autoscaling or autohealing, and every instance drifts as scripts or images change.

choices.text: An instance template plus a regional MIG with autoscaling and health-check autohealing
choices.rationale: The template guarantees identical VMs, the regional MIG spreads them across zones, autoscaling adds or removes capacity, and autohealing recreates instances that fail health checks.

choices.text: An unmanaged instance group with a fixed number of VMs registered as backends
choices.rationale: Unmanaged groups can be load balancer backends but do not support autoscaling, autohealing, rolling updates, multi-zone placement or instance templates.

choices.text: A single large VM resized vertically as load grows, fronted by the load balancer
choices.rationale: One VM is a single point of failure, resizing needs a restart, and nothing recreates it automatically if it fails.

prompt: EHR Healthcare must retain control over the encryption keys protecting patient data stored in BigQuery and Cloud Storage, including the ability to rotate and revoke keys on their own schedule, while still using Google-managed storage services. Which approach meets this requirement?

choices.text: Google-managed default encryption at rest, which already protects both services
choices.rationale: Default encryption protects the data, but the customer cannot manage rotation, disable the key or audit its use, so it does not meet the control requirement.

choices.text: Customer-managed encryption keys held in Cloud KMS and attached to the datasets and buckets
choices.rationale: CMEK lets the customer set the rotation period, trigger rotation, and disable or destroy keys to cut off access, while BigQuery and Cloud Storage keep doing the encryption.

choices.text: Application-layer client-side encryption only, with keys kept in an internal wiki page
choices.rationale: Keys kept outside a key management service lose rotation, access control and audit logging, and the managed services' own encryption stays outside the customer's control.

choices.text: Turning off encryption at rest on the datasets and buckets to simplify key management for the team
choices.rationale: Encryption at rest cannot be turned off on Google Cloud, and removing it would violate the healthcare compliance goal anyway.

prompt: A regulated company wants to prevent data in BigQuery and Cloud Storage from being exfiltrated to projects outside their trusted boundary, even if an insider has valid IAM credentials. They need a logical perimeter around these API-based services. Which control addresses this directly?

choices.text: VPC firewall rules that deny egress from the VMs that run the data pipelines
choices.rationale: Firewalls work at the network layer on VM traffic. They do not govern API calls to Google-managed services such as BigQuery or Cloud Storage.

choices.text: VPC Service Controls service perimeters around the BigQuery and Cloud Storage projects
choices.rationale: A perimeter blocks operations such as copying data to buckets or tables outside the boundary even when the caller holds valid IAM permissions or stolen credentials.

choices.text: Organization Policy constraints that restrict the locations where resources are created
choices.rationale: A location constraint governs where resources can be created. It does not stop data being copied to a project outside the trusted boundary.

choices.text: IAM Conditions that only allow access during defined business hours and weekdays
choices.rationale: A time condition narrows when access is allowed, but an insider with valid credentials can still exfiltrate data inside the permitted window.

prompt: You are hardening service-account usage for workloads running in GKE and for CI/CD pipelines deploying to Google Cloud. Which two practices follow Google's security best practices? Choose two.

choices.text: Federate the CI/CD identity with Workload Identity Federation so it gets short-lived credentials
choices.rationale: Federation gives external workloads temporary credentials tied to their own identity provider, so no long-lived service account key is ever exported.

choices.text: Download a service-account JSON key and commit it to the pipeline repository for the convenience of developers
choices.rationale: Google recommends avoiding service account keys. A key committed to a repository is a long-lived credential that anyone with repository access can reuse.

choices.text: Grant narrowly scoped predefined or custom roles to each service account instead of Owner or Editor
choices.rationale: Granting only the permissions a workload needs limits the damage if its service account is compromised; broad basic roles should be avoided.

choices.text: Reuse one highly privileged service account across all workloads to simplify management
choices.rationale: Sharing one account across applications blurs audit trails and widens the blast radius. Best practice is a single-purpose service account per workload.

choices.text: Grant the Owner role to every service account to avoid permission errors during rollout
choices.rationale: Owner is a basic role with sweeping permissions. Handing it out to avoid errors is the opposite of least privilege.

prompt: A retailer runs a steady, predictable baseline of Compute Engine workloads 24/7, plus spiky batch jobs. They want to cut the cost of the always-on baseline without sacrificing availability. Which optimization is most appropriate for the steady baseline?

choices.text: Move the entire steady baseline onto Spot VMs to get the deepest discount
choices.rationale: Spot VMs can be preempted at any time, which would break the always-on availability requirement. They suit the fault-tolerant batch jobs instead.

choices.text: Buy committed use discounts sized to the steady baseline, keeping spiky jobs uncommitted
choices.rationale: Commitments of one or three years suit predictable usage and discount it without changing availability. Sizing them to the baseline avoids paying for idle commitment on the spiky work.

choices.text: Keep the baseline on on-demand pricing so capacity can be changed at any time without commitment
choices.rationale: On-demand is the highest-priced option for usage that is known to be steady, so it forgoes savings the predictability makes available.

choices.text: Shut the baseline down every night and restart it each morning to cut billed hours
choices.rationale: The requirement says the baseline runs 24/7 without sacrificing availability, so a nightly shutdown breaks the requirement.

prompt: Logs are written to Cloud Storage and accessed heavily for 30 days, rarely after 90 days, and must be retained for 7 years for audit. You want to minimize storage cost automatically without an external scheduler. What should you configure?

choices.text: Keep every object in Standard storage for the whole seven-year retention period
choices.rationale: Standard has the highest at-rest cost, and most of these objects are rarely read after 90 days, so it overpays for years.

choices.text: Lifecycle rules moving objects from Standard to Nearline, then Coldline or Archive, as they age
choices.rationale: Cloud Storage evaluates lifecycle rules itself and supports Standard to Nearline, Coldline or Archive transitions, so no scheduler is needed and the data stays available for the seven years.

choices.text: A nightly Cloud Function that copies aging objects into buckets of a colder storage class
choices.rationale: This rebuilds a built-in feature as custom code to maintain, with copy operations and extra failure modes, when lifecycle rules do it natively.

choices.text: A lifecycle Delete rule that removes objects after 90 days to keep the bucket small and cheap
choices.rationale: Deleting at 90 days cuts cost but destroys data the audit requirement says must be kept for seven years.

prompt: A global web application serves mostly static assets plus some dynamic API calls and suffers high latency for users far from the origin region. Which two changes will most improve global performance? Choose two.

choices.text: Enable Cloud CDN on the external Application Load Balancer to cache static assets at the edge
choices.rationale: Cloud CDN serves cacheable responses from Google edge locations near users, so cache hits avoid the long trip to the origin region.

choices.text: Use a global external Application Load Balancer with one anycast IP, ending users at the nearest edge
choices.rationale: It terminates HTTP(S) as close to users as possible and routes over Google's network to the closest healthy backend, cutting latency for dynamic calls that cannot be cached.

choices.text: Consolidate every backend onto a single zonal VM in the origin region to simplify operations
choices.rationale: One zonal VM keeps all users far from the origin and also removes redundancy, which worsens both latency and availability.

choices.text: Disable HTTP keep-alive on the backends so each request negotiates a fresh connection
choices.rationale: Without connection reuse every request pays the extra handshake round trips, which raises latency instead of lowering it.

choices.text: Serve every asset directly from the origin VM's local disk across the public internet
choices.rationale: This is the slow path being optimized away: no caching, no edge termination, and every distant user pays full origin latency.

prompt: KnightMotives Automotive keeps the orders for its unreliable build-to-order system in a self-managed MySQL database in its data center. The team must move it to Cloud SQL for MySQL with minimal downtime, using continuous replication to keep the target in sync until cutover. Which Google tool is purpose-built for this?

choices.text: Database Migration Service using a continuous job: initial load plus ongoing change replication
choices.rationale: A continuous job copies the data then streams changes into Cloud SQL, so you wait for replication lag to approach zero, stop writes and promote, keeping cutover downtime short.

choices.text: A one-time mysqldump export imported into Cloud SQL during an extended maintenance window
choices.rationale: A dump is a point-in-time copy, so writes made after the export are lost unless the source stays offline for the whole export and import.

choices.text: Storage Transfer Service jobs that copy the database's data files into Cloud Storage for a later restore
choices.rationale: Copying files gives a point-in-time snapshot with no ongoing replication, and it never produces a Cloud SQL instance. Storage Transfer Service moves objects between storage systems rather than replicating a live database.

choices.text: BigQuery Data Transfer Service scheduled loads from the MySQL server into BigQuery tables for reporting
choices.rationale: This service loads data into BigQuery on a schedule. The target here is Cloud SQL for MySQL, and scheduled loads are not continuous replication.

prompt: A company is exposing internal services as managed external APIs and needs developer onboarding, quota/rate limiting, OAuth-based security, analytics, and monetization. Which Google Cloud product is designed for full API lifecycle management?

choices.text: Cloud Endpoints, using ESPv2 proxies that are deployed in front of every backend service
choices.rationale: Endpoints provides authentication, quota management, monitoring and logging through ESPv2, but its documented feature set has no integrated developer portal or monetization.

choices.text: Apigee API management, including its developer portal, analytics and monetization plans
choices.rationale: Apigee covers the full API lifecycle: developer portal, quotas and spike arrest, OAuth and API key security, built-in analytics, and monetization with rate plans.

choices.text: Cloud Load Balancing URL maps routing each API path to the backend service that owns it
choices.rationale: URL maps only route requests. They provide no developer onboarding, quotas, OAuth policy or monetization.

choices.text: Cloud Armor security policies attached to the load balancer in front of all the APIs
choices.rationale: Cloud Armor filters hostile traffic at the edge. It is not an API management platform and has no onboarding, analytics or monetization.

prompt: An SRE team wants to quantify reliability and decide objectively when to slow feature releases versus invest in stability. They define availability targets and track the gap between target and actual to govern release pace. Which set of concepts are they applying?

choices.text: SLIs measure behavior, SLOs set targets, and the error budget (1 - SLO) governs release pace
choices.rationale: An SLI measures performance, an SLO is the target for it, and the error budget is the tolerated failure. When it is nearly depleted, risky changes are held back in favor of reliability.

choices.text: Service quotas, resource limits and billing alerts that cap capacity and spend per project
choices.rationale: Quotas and billing alerts control capacity and cost. They say nothing about whether users are getting reliable service.

choices.text: RTO, RPO and backup retention targets that define how fast and how completely services recover
choices.rationale: These are disaster-recovery objectives that apply after a major incident, not steady-state reliability targets for governing release pace.

choices.text: IAM roles, bindings and conditions that define who may deploy changes to production
choices.rationale: IAM controls who can act, not how reliable the service is or when to slow releases.

prompt: You are establishing observability for a production GKE platform and want proactive detection plus the ability to investigate incidents quickly. Which two actions reflect Google Cloud operations best practices? Choose two.

choices.text: Alerting policies in Cloud Monitoring on SLO burn rate and user-facing symptoms, sent to notification channels
choices.rationale: Policies on metrics, logs or SLO burn rate notify the on-call team before users escalate, which is what proactive detection means.

choices.text: Centralized Cloud Logging with log-based metrics and sinks that route logs to long-term storage
choices.rationale: Aggregated sinks centralize logs across projects and can route them to Cloud Storage or BigQuery, and log-based metrics turn log patterns into alertable signals, supporting fast investigation.

choices.text: Turn off production logging to cut noise and cost, relying on dashboards and metrics alone for diagnosis
choices.rationale: Without logs there is no record of what happened, so incident investigation becomes guesswork.

choices.text: Depend on engineers opening the dashboards manually a few times each day to spot problems
choices.rationale: Manual checks are reactive and leave off-hours problems undetected until users report them.

choices.text: Begin collecting metrics only after users report an incident, to avoid ongoing overhead
choices.rationale: The data needed to see the problem build up is missing by then, which defeats the purpose of observability.
